thread.title: Is Amazon Investing Enough in Autonomous Driving?

author: David Marino-Nachison
title: Is Amazon Investing Enough in Autonomous Driving?
text:
Photo: AFP/Getty Images By David Marino-Nachison Updated Sept. 25, 2018 4:01 p.m. ET It’s time for Amazon.com (ticker: AMZN) to become a car company.
OK, not quite. But it does need to invest in autonomous driving to protect its retail business from companies that work with Waymo, the autonomous-car company owned by Google parent Alphabet (GOOGL), to develop on-demand delivery offerings, according to Morgan Stanley analyst Brian Nowak.
Small, slow and super cheap: China's low-speed electric vehicles, or LSEVs, are bringing the thrill of driving to the masses—and hampering the government's efforts to develop an upscale EV industry. Image: Crystal Tai The notion comes as investors have lately contemplated multibillion-dollar valuations for the autonomous divisions at other high-profile companies. They’ve got plenty to gain, including the possibility of helping develop businesses that challenge Amazon’s efforts to conquer last-mile delivery, but what does Amazon have to lose?
Here’s some context. Morgan Stanley valued Tesla (TSLA) at nearly $18 billion earlier this month, and in August it envisioned a $175 billion value for Waymo , including $90 billion for a logistics business that might work with retailers. Evercore ISI posited $100 billion for Waymo. (Want to read about an Apple (AAPL) car? We’ve got you covered .)
Nowak didn’t cook up a valuation for a potential Amazon operation, but he suggested that the company has good reasons for investing in one:
Newsletter Sign-up • Waymo wouldn’t necessarily be a Prime killer—but it could give competitors a boost, he wrote.
“We see the potential for a deeper integration between Google Shopping and Waymo autonomous cars to deliver retailers’ in-store (or warehouse) inventory to consumers in 1-2 hours,” Nowak wrote. “Waymo could effectively offer retailers an inexpensive way to compete with Amazon’s Prime Now.”
A popular and growing Prime product should still be a “differentiator” for Amazon, Nowak wrote. But “Waymo could help retailers level the playing field on inventory/selection, shipping cost/speed and, thereby, the ability to invest in price,” he said.
• And autonomous technology could lower Amazon’s long-haul shipping costs by as much as 50%, according to Nowak. He sees Amazon’s shipping costs growing at a compounded annual growth rate of 27% through 2022, hitting $75 billion.
In other words, Amazon could use the technology to stem the tide. “Amazon’s ability to build a differentiated autonomous offering could lead to around 5% to 15% (around $10-$30 billion) higher gross profit dollars…to either reinvest or flow down to higher free cash flow,” he wrote.
Recommended Reading What’s Waymo Worth? Tesla’s Ahead of the Competition. Can It Stay in Front? Four Reasons Tesla Mobility Is Worth a Lot Less Than Alphabet’s Waymo How much should Amazon spend? Nowak didn’t detail a figure, though he notes that other companies have spent amounts in the single-digit billions and suggests that even matching Alphabet’s lifetime funding of Waymo would represent only a fraction of Amazon’s retail expenses.
And it’s perhaps the case that Amazon could just work with other companies that develop technology it thinks can help—whether that means Waymo, or someone else. Whatever the case, Amazon has some clear interest in owning more steps in the delivery process . (Though Barron’s Teresa Rivas recently covered one analysis suggesting investors may overestimate its threat to the big parcel companies .)
In an email responding to our questions about the notion that Amazon should invest more, a spokeswoman pointed to the company’s efforts in drone delivery and its participation in a Toyota program , announced in January, to develop a concept vehicle meant to meet the needs of future communities and businesses.
